source.title_on_document: Searching together: Human–AI complementarities in innovation search

supplement.holds: No supplementary material is mentioned. Appendix 1 (interviewee list) and Appendix 2 (secondary sources) are in this PDF (pp. 14-15). Data availability: 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' (p. 15)

paper_design_summary: Exploratory qualitative study. The authors ran 41 semi-structured interviews (1422 minutes) with employees of an AI search-services firm ('Firm AI') and with innovation managers and R&D staff in 25 client organizations and one non-client organization, and added 64 secondary articles (blogs, customer stories, online articles) on AI search tools. They coded the material with a Gioia-style grounded-theory approach into three human-AI 'relational dialectics'; no output is produced or scored and no one is assigned to AI.

studies.label: Qualitative interview study of AI use in corporate innovation search (41 interviews, 27 organizations) plus secondary articles

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. Organizations were selected by purposeful and network sampling through Firm AI's customer network; interviewees were people already using AI in innovation search.
assignment.quote: We used an exploratory qualitative research design to identify emerging complementarities between humans and AI in innovation search.

participants.exclusions: No people count is stated in the text. The paper reports 41 interviews (some interviewees had 2 rounds; one interview had 2 interviewees, M17A/B) across 27 companies. Appendix 1 lists position codes F1-F5 and M1-M34 (M17 = two people), but the paper never states a number of distinct interviewees, so n is left null. Secondary data: 64 articles.
participants.who: Firm AI employees (CEO, developers, business development, scouting) and innovation managers, R&D managers, CIOs, chief scientists, and four non-managerial innovation/R&D team members in client firms; one non-client firm.
participants.country: Organizations across Europe, the USA, the UK, and the Middle East (Netherlands, Germany, Belgium, Switzerland, Finland, Sweden, Italy, UK, United States, Saudi Arabia per Appendix 1).
participants.quote: In total, we conducted 41 interviews, amounting to 1422 min (see Appendix 1), with an average duration of 35 min per interview.
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 2, Section 1 ('27 companies'); p. 4, Section 3.1 ('25 large organizations'); p. 14, Appendix 1

ai_tool.name_model: Alpha AI (Firm AI's NLP search system over scientific publications, patents, and company websites); interviewees were also invited to reflect on generative AI tools such as ChatGPT; secondary data cover Azure OpenAI service, Amazon Kendra, Glean chat.
ai_tool.how_used: Used by firms in their ordinary innovation search (technology scouting, solution search), either by Firm AI on behalf of clients or by clients on the Alpha platform; the study records interviewees' reflections, not use under study conditions.

task.description: Corporate innovation search (technology scouting, knowledge and solution search) as described by interviewees; no task was administered.
task.duration: Interviews averaged 35 minutes (1422 minutes total); data collection spanned the period before and after the emergence of large language models (study designed early 2022).

company_involvement.description: The sample was built through Firm AI, a European AI search-services firm: its employees were interviewed (F1-F5) and its customer network supplied the 25 client organizations. No funding by Firm AI is stated, and the authors declare no competing interests.
company_involvement.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 14, Appendix 1 and Declaration of competing interest

eligibility.reason: Qualitative interview study (41 interviews, 27 organizations) coded with grounded theory. No one is assigned to AI, no creative output is produced or scored, and there is no comparison with and without AI. The number of distinct interviewees is not stated (about 40 position codes in Appendix 1), below 50 in any case and not an experimental sample. It is not an AI-versus-human output comparison and has no diversity, novelty, or originality outcome, so it does not fit the observational context class either.

one_line_finding: From 41 interviews in 27 organizations (p. 5, Section 3.1; Appendix 1, p. 14), the authors describe three human-AI dialectics in innovation search (human-centered vs boundary-spanning search, contextualizing vs decontextualizing, judging vs envisaging) and argue they expand rationality and mitigate bias; no quantitative creativity outcome is reported.
open_questions: Whether qualitative interview studies should be listed in the screening report under a named exclusion reason (the codebook's list covers model-only, theory, self-report-only, and perception studies, but not qualitative interviews explicitly).
notes: Exclude from the core dataset and from context. Interview-based perceptions only; the closest codebook exclusion is 'studies whose only outcome is self-reported'. Appendix 1 row numbers skip 4 and 13, consistent with second-round interviews of F1 and M6 ('2 rounds'). The candidates.json design guess 'other' is consistent with this reading.
